opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was mostly a practical decision. The offline step in HippoRAG is where we take every passage in the corpus and run open information extraction over it: named entities first, then subject–relation–object triples. Those triples become the nodes and edges of the knowledge graph that plays the role of the hippocampal index. Everything downstream depends on that graph being reasonably good, so we needed a model that could do OpenIE well with just a few-shot prompt, no task-specific training.

At the time, GPT-3.5 Turbo hit a nice sweet spot. It was strong enough at following a structured extraction format and pulling out meaningful entities and relations, and it was cheap and fast enough to run over tens of thousands of passages without blowing the budget. GPT-4 would probably have given somewhat cleaner triples, but indexing is something you pay for across the entire corpus, so cost scales quickly. For a research prototype where we wanted to iterate, 3.5 was the reasonable choice.

We also didn't want the method to look like it only worked because of one proprietary model, so we ran ablations with open models. Llama-3 variants, for example, did fairly comparably. That was reassuring, because it suggested the gains come from the architecture: building the graph, linking query entities into it, and running Personalized PageRank. They don't come from some special property of GPT-3.5. And practically, it means people can run the indexing step with open models if they care about cost or privacy.

So the short version is that GPT-3.5 was good enough at extraction, affordable at corpus scale, and we checked that the approach wasn't overly tied to it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it mostly came down to cost. The offline indexing phase in HippoRAG is where we run OpenIE over the entire corpus, so for every passage we're asking the model to extract named entities and then triples, and that's a lot of calls. When we were building this, GPT-3.5 Turbo was a very capable extractor that was still cheap enough to index corpora with tens of thousands of passages without blowing through our academic budget. GPT-4 would have given us cleaner, more complete knowledge graphs, but running it over everything was just not realistic for us at the time.

The other thing is that we actually wanted to show the method works even with a somewhat noisy graph. The whole hippocampal indexing idea is that the graph doesn't need to be perfect, because Personalized PageRank spreads activation over the structure and you still recover the right passages even if some triples are missing or a bit off. So using a mid-tier model was partly a feature, since it demonstrated the robustness. And we did ablate this. We tried smaller open models like Llama 3 8B for the extraction, and performance dropped but it didn't collapse, and when we tried stronger models the retrieval got better, which is kind of what you'd hope. The method scales with the extractor rather than being bottlenecked by it.

So the short answer is GPT-3.5 was the sweet spot between extraction quality, cost, and speed for an offline phase that has to touch every document in the collection.

sol-6.1.text: We chose GPT-3.5 mainly because it offered a good balance between extraction quality and cost. In the offline stage, we use the model to extract entities and relations from passages and build the knowledge graph, so we need to run it across the whole corpus. Using a more expensive model would make that indexing process substantially more costly. GPT-3.5 was capable enough for that task, and it let us explore how much we could gain from the retrieval architecture itself.
